newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - API shows surprising uptick in refinery use.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - API shows surprising uptick in refinery use.

text.p: REUTER SURVEY ESTIMATES* ACTUAL STOCKS FOR
FOR WEEK ENDED 05/16/97 WEEK ENDED 05/16/97-CHANGE
CRUDE...........DN 2.50 million bbls 315,811 UP 5.935 MLN
DISTILLATE......UP 1.50 million bbls 98,379 UP 1.917 MLN
UTILIZATION... UNCH/DOWN 1.0 pct 97.6 UP 0.7 PCT
The highlight of the American Petroleum Institute's weekly status report was an unexpected step up in refinery utilization from an already high level, analysts said Tuesday.

"It could get ugly for gasoline because we are slamming crude through refineries, and while demand is good, after a while it will not be enough to absorb all the supply we may get," said Pat Hughes, analyst with Chevron Corp in California.
"It looks like bad news for products," said Hughes.

Refinery usage was up at 97.6 percent last week, compared with 96.9 percent the previous week, the API said. That was the highest level for this time of year in at least four years, an API official said.

Oddly, however, and another of the anomolies which have been apparent in the API's data in recent months, gasoline production was slightly down on the week at 7.959 million barrels per day (bpd) from 8.109 million bpd the previous week.

Gasoline stocks overall rose 837,000 barrels to 197.8 million barrels, while "implied demand" for gasoline -- the sum of output and imports, minus any rise in stocks -- was at around 8.2 million barrels a day. (API has been showing gasoline "demand" running well above the the Department of Energy).

Meanwhile, crude oil inventories fell a sharp 5.935 million barrels last week, according to the API. But that represented a swing back from the previous week's questionable 6.9 million-barrel rise and the API revised the crude stocks number for the week ended May 9 from 322.6 millin to 321.7 million.

So, the net change since the beginning of May is a rise in crude stocks nationwide of 600,000 barrels and analysts said the main thing to focus on is the fact that stocks are some 20 million barrels higher than the same time last year.
Analysts disagreed on the interpretation of the conflicting data.

"(Crude) imports should be easing now that production is shut for maintenance abroad and run rates are high. They are running about 98 percent in the (U.S.) Gulf now," said Al Lindseth, manager for oil and gas hedge programs at GSC Energy in Atlanta.
"We should start to see demand (for gasoline) stabilize at these levels since Memorial Day weekend provides a kickstart," said Lindseth.
Crude futures in after-hours trading on NYMEX's ACCESS system ticked up, with July futures rising 21 cents to $21.80 a barrel.
However, one New York trader said the gain came on a single 100-lot order ahead of the API figures and there was thin volume at the higher level.

"After the API reversal last week I think we would have needed much more bullish numbers to sustain or at least extend gains that we have made. I think crude will continue in a correction," said a New York crude trader.
Heating oil and gasoline futures were mixed in thin trading on ACCESS. June contracts ended down 0.28 at 57.64 cents a gallon and up 0.18 at 65.39 cents a gallon, respectively.
*The Reuter survey is a simple average of a poll of at least half a dozen leading analysts, omitting the high and low numbers.
